document.title: Pre-filed Statement of Marjorie Rosenbluth Philips, Senior Vice President of Wholesale Market Policy for LS Power Development, LLC, for the PJM Governance…
document.group: PJM governance and stakeholder reform vote

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
 
 
 
 
 
PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms 
) 
)
) 
 
 
 Docket No. AD26-7-000  
 
 
                                     
 
 PRE-TECHNICAL CONFERENCE COMMENTS OF MARJORIE PHILIPS, LS 
POWER DEVELOPMENT, LLC  
I. Introduction 
LS Power Development, LLC (“LS Power”) appreciates the opportunity to 
participate in this examination of the efficacy of PJM Interconnection LLC (“PJM”) 
governance structure.1 Founded in 1990, LS Power is a premier development, 
investment, and operating company focused on the North American power and 
energy infrastructure sector, with leading platforms across generation, transmission 
and energy expansion solutions. Since inception, LS Power has developed or 
acquired 50,000 MW of power generation, including utility-scale solar, wind, hydro, 
battery energy storage, and natural gas-fired facilities. Through its transmission 
business, LS Power Grid, the company operates 7 transmission utilities, has built 
780+ miles of high-voltage transmission with another 400+ miles currently in 
construction or development. LS Power actively invests in and scales businesses that 
are meeting the growing needs of the energy expansion, including electric vehicle 
charging, demand response, microgrids, renewable fuels and waste-to-energy 
platforms. Over the years, LS Power has raised more than $85 billion in debt and 
equity capital to support North American infrastructure. LS Power has been an active 
participant in PJM for three decades.   
Every stakeholder, whether Member and non-Member has had grievances with the 
PJM governance process at one point or another, but the bottom line is that Members, 
the Board, and the relevant regulatory bodies should be proud: PJM’s 
 
1 All terms used herein shall have the meaning set forth in the PJM Operating Agreement.  PJM, 
Amended and Restated Operating Agreement, Rate Schedule FERC No. 24, (eff. 7/14/2011) 
(“Operating Agreement”).

LS Power Comments 
Page 2 
 
“constitutional” documents have allowed PJM to evolve over more than thirty years 
while maintaining reliability through independent and competitive markets.   
Considering the unprecedented growth in data center demand, all market 
participants, including PJM, are having to reconsider how their past programs can 
be improved to meet rapidly developing needs and stability for the future. We are all 
doing so while trying to balance enhanced stakeholder engagement up and down the 
value chain. And so, we must ask here, is PJMs present need to make adjustment 
one of fundamental governance reform or just another step-change aligned with the 
governance structures which have served the region well over time?  
In answering this question, we find that the unanticipated resource adequacy issue 
facing PJM (amongst others) is not fundamentally one of governance. While record 
unanticipated load growth associated with data center development is a matter of 
critical importance - ranging from national security to everyday personal use - 
addressing this need is more logically addressed through the lens of stable market 
rules, efficient interconnection queues, supply chain constraints and broader 
permitting regimes, rather than PJM governance.  
While it is true that PJM did not have or in some cases, did not robustly follow the 
rules in place to facilitate and manage this unanticipated load growth,  it is also true 
that no amount of governance reform today can change the physical reality that it 
presently takes roughly five years to bring a new combined-cycle plant online, and 
considerably longer for coal and nuclear facilities, not to mention getting 
transmission upgrades built.  
Driving the governance discussion is the concern policy makers have expressed: 
they lack access to the Board, and it is not independent of stakeholder influence.  
This is a false narrative.  Policy makers and Members already have access to the 
Board; policy makers through the Organization of PJM States (“OPSI”) meetings, 
and Members through the Liaison Committee.  The states are not restricted by ex 
parte rules that apply to stakeholders.  Furthermore, all these parties can participate 
in stakeholder proceedings, and any interested party can send a letter to the Board 
expressing its opinion, which is then shared publicly.  Indeed, PJM has filed joint 
proposals with state utility commissions and representatives of governors have made 
presentations in the stakeholder process.2 
 
2 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER25-1357-000, "Proposal for Revised Price Cap and Price Floor for the 
2026/2027 and 2027/2028 Delivery Years, and Request for a Waiver of the 60-Days' Notice Requirement to Allow 
for a March 31, 2025 Effective Date," filed February 20, 2025. See also https://www.pjm.com/-
/media/DotCom/committees-groups/committees/mrc/2025/20250618/20250618-item-04---3-sub-annual-capacity-
market---presentation.pdf

LS Power Comments 
Page 3 
 
What PJM’s governance structure can offer in times of robust growth is a stable 
regulatory forum for decision-making, one which continues to be deeply invested in 
providing the regulatory certainty and price-signals required to allow stakeholders 
to make multi-decade investments in U.S. wholesale power infrastructure possible. 
With that said, opportunities exist to enhance PJM’s existing governance structure 
to ensure better transparency, policy maker input, and stakeholder alignment while 
preserving PJM’s independence and mission to ensure reliability through 
competitive markets. 
II. The Board and PJM’s Jurisdictional Authority 
Our comments are grounded in the jurisdictional and regulatory limits that apply to 
the Commission, PJM, and the states. The Federal Power Act does not speak in terms 
of “affordability.” Instead, it requires FERC to judge whether a rate is “just and 
reasonable” — a standard that turns on the relationship between a seller’s costs and 
market position (market power), and the price that seller charges.3 “Affordability,” 
by contrast, is a qualitative judgment about the impact of a rate on the buyer, and 
turns on the relationship between a customer’s income and its retail bill. 
This distinction is why it is critical that the PJM Board focuses on producing 
wholesale market outcomes that are just and reasonable, while the states focus on 
how those market outcomes are then allocated — equitably or otherwise — to their 
retail constituents. Keeping these two distinct responsibilities straight and keeping 
them with the entities who jurisdictionally manage them, is foundational to 
everything that follows.4  Addressing the present significant load growth challenge 
will require hyperscalers, state and federal regulators, PJM, the PJM Board, 
transmission and generation asset owners and developers, end users, transmission 
dependent utilities and consumer advocates to work cooperatively to implement 
rules and regulations in the RTO, at the federal and at the state levels to manage this 
 
3 Federal Power Act § 206(a), 16 U.S.C. § 824e(a) (2018). 
4  “We recognize that states have exclusive authority over resource planning and the generation mix within their 
boundaries. Nothing about our preliminary finding here, however, intrudes or is intended to intrude on that exclusive 
authority.” New York Independent System Operator, Inc., 195 FERC ¶61,216, at ¶93 (2026).  
See also Commissioner LaCerte concurrence: To that end, and in light of our action in today’s orders, I also ask the 
state public utility commissions—whether they have already approved large load retail tariffs, are in the process of 
crafting large load retail tariffs, or have yet to embark on this essential tariff design process—to take a hard look and 
ensure their large load retail tariff provisions insulate ratepayers from the negative impacts of data center growth. 
Additionally, I expect PJM to design proposals in response to this show cause order that dovetail with the efforts on 
the retail side to implement the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, protect customers, and ensure that large loads cover the 
costs they incur to integrate with the grid. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 195 FERC ¶ 61,211 (2026) (LaCerte, 
Comm'r, concurring at 3).

LS Power Comments 
Page 4 
 
new grid reality while ensuring PJM fulfills its missions of maintaining reliability 
through competitive markets.  Our recommendations below are offered in 
recognition of those jurisdictional realities and in the core understanding that 
cooperation and coordination is imperative to success. 
The three pillars of PJM governance, the Open Access Transmission Tariff, the 
Operating Agreement and the Consolidated Transmission Owners Agreement 
(“CTOA”), are each foundational documents upon which PJM was approved and 
has operated for three decades.  Section 3.1 of the Operating Agreement provides 
that the purpose of the LLC (PJM) is “to operate in accordance with FERC 
requirements as an Independent System Operator, comprised of the PJM Board, the 
Office of the Interconnection, and the Members Committee, with the authorities and 
responsibilities set forth in this Agreement.”5  The Members Committee is an 
integral part of PJM as an Independent System Operator.  No single FERC approved 
document regarding PJM’s formation is more important than the other, and each 
holds equal authority in the ongoing operation and governance of PJM.  Any 
assertion to the contrary does not appropriately reflect the foundation of PJM.6   This 
deliberately crafted allocation and balance among the parties is what has contributed 
to PJM’s success; any action that significantly tilts this balance in order to meet the 
moment must be considered judiciously so that it does not undermine PJM’s overall 
success. 
III. Board Independence 
Section 7.7 (i) of the Operating Agreement places the duty on the PJM Board to 
ensure “that a Member or group of Members shall not have undue influence over the 
operation of the PJM Region.”   
Note that the discussion around who has 205 rights applies only to the Operating 
Agreement.  With respect to resource adequacy, PJM has exclusive 205 rights under 
the Reliability Assurance Agreement (“RAA”).  Under the Operating Agreement, 
on the other hand, for matters that pertain to the energy market and regional 
transmission planning protocols, when the Members Committee reaches a 2/3 sector 
weighted vote, PJM is expected and indeed, required, to respect that vote and file 
 
5 Operating Agreement Section 3.1. 
6 Furthermore, the CTOA itself indicates that the Operating Agreement, which is controlled by the PJM Members 
Committee, is foundational.  Section 3.1 of the CTOA states:  Prior to [the CTOA] becoming effective as to any 
such entity, each of the following events shall have occurred: i. The Operating Agreement is in full force and effect.   
ii. The Operating Agreement has been executed by the entity.  iii. [The CTOA] has been executed by the entity. iv. 
All required regulatory approvals have been obtained.

LS Power Comments 
Page 5 
 
the passed Members Committee language with the Commission acting in an 
administrative capacity, accordingly.7  The Operating Agreement also provides the 
PJM Board explicit powers to comment, either on its own initiative or at the request 
of a PJM User Group, on proposed Operating Agreement changes as it moves 
through the stakeholder process or to submit directly to the Members Committee 
proposed Operating Agreement language8. State Policy Makers, for their part, hold 
no formal voting rights, but they nonetheless exercise considerable influence over 
PJM outcomes.9 
Given this structure, Board independence means that when the Board reaches a 
decision, it must weigh the full range of views expressed by these constituencies and 
then act independently and consistently with its mandate and PJM’s governing 
agreements. PJM Board independence is not only a governance imperative for just 
and reasonable rates, but also an imperative to the long-term health of the market.  
Some are concerned with Board independence and transparency and have proposed 
that the Board hold open meetings.10 For the PJM Board to continue to enjoy 
independence requires them to continue to exercise their role with the highest ability 
to conduct fulsome deliberations which can only be afforded by maintaining closed 
Board sessions. LS Power is concerned that honest deliberation will be muted if 
Board members believe they are being judged for the appearance of favoring a 
particular position, and that open sessions risk becoming performative rather than 
substantive. The same reasoning counsels against disclosing individual votes.  
Nonetheless, we see room for meaningful improvement short of full PJM Board 
transparency or a change in the way Section 205 rights are allocated.  LS Power’s 
recommendations include: 
 
7 Duquesne Light Co. v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 176 FERC ¶ 61,052 at PP 26-27 (2021).  The Members 
Committee can file Section 205 Operating Agreement language changes directly with FERC today without PJM’s 
administrative function.  PJM also acts in a purely administrative capacity when filing Section 205 filings for PJM 
Tariff revisions for PJM Transmission Owners. 
8 Section 7.7(v) of the Operating Agreement explicitly provides the PJM Board with the authority to “on its own 
initiative or at the request of a User Group as specified in this Operating Agreement, submit to the Members 
Committee such proposed amendments to this Agreement or any Schedule herein, or proposed new Schedule, as it 
may deem appropriate.” 
 
9 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER25-1357-000, "Proposal for Revised Price Cap and Price Floor for the 
2026/2027 and 2027/2028 Delivery Years, and Request for a Waiver of the 60-Days' Notice Requirement to Allow 
for a March 31, 2025 Effective Date," filed February 20, 2025Cite to PAPUC VRR proposal; see also 
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/committees/mrc/2025/20250618/20250618-item-04---3-
sub-annual-capacity-market---presentation.pdf  
10 Kavulla, Problems in Electricity Market Governance: An Assessment,” R Street Policy Study No. 180 (Oct. 
2019), p. 11 (“Kavulla Report).

LS Power Comments 
Page 6 
 
● Require the Board to explain its reasoning.11 Companies like ours are 
investing billions of dollars in this market, and we need confidence that Board 
decision-making is consistent over time. That confidence is undermined when 
the Board takes actions inconsistent over time with no explanation.12  The 
Board should be required to explain the basis for the given position and 
provide sound reasoning especially when it reverses course. 
● Relax the ex parte rules that apply to Board-stakeholder interactions. Other 
RTOs build in structured, direct Board interaction with stakeholders — for 
example, quarterly meetings with individual sectors — and PJM should 
consider a similar approach. 
● Adopt the ISO-NE model of assigning a Board member to each state.13 That 
Board member would be responsible for maintaining a regular outreach 
schedule with state representatives, potentially extending to the state’s utility 
commission or the governor’s office. This would give states the level of direct 
Board access that some have said they currently lack.  It would also provide 
the Board with insight into interests that are particular to a given state and 
worth considering in deliberations.  That said, these interactions should not 
undermine the independence requirement of Board decisions. Having this 
unique structure in place also enhances state engagement in a way that is not 
available to stakeholders.  
● Create a Market Surveillance Committee along the lines of the CAISO.14 This 
Committee would be comprised of independent individuals with expertise in 
electricity market design (with an emphasis on independence), who advise the 
Board on decisions.  This could help break the perceived cycle of when PJM 
proposes to modify an existing rule to ensure efficient price outcomes 
stakeholders narrowly focus on their economic interest rather than the benefit 
 
11 Kavulla Report, p. 14. 
12 See https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/about-pjm/who-we-are/public-disclosures/2024/20240919-pjm-board-
response-consumer-advocates-letter-re-urgent-reforms-pjm-capacity-market-re-reliability-must-run-units.pdf and 
subsequent change in position (issued September 19, 2024) and a subsequent reverse in position in December in a 
FERC filing PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER25-682-000, "Revisions to Reliability Pricing Model," 
filed December 9, 2024 
13 “Additionally, the Nominating and Governance Committee of the ISO-NE Board assigns two Board members to 
serve as liaisons between the Board and each state commission. The Board liaisons and the state commissions meet 
at least once per year, every six to eight months, depending on the interest of the state commission and the 
availability of the liaisons.[35] NESCOE, NECPUC, or state officials can request meetings with the Board as 
needed.”  Governance Structure and Practices in the FERC Jurisdictional ISOs/RTOs February 2021, Prepared for 
NESCOE by: Christopher A. Parent Katherine S. Fisher, William R. Cotton, Cali C. Clar, Exeter Associates, Inc. 
(February 2021), Section 3.2.2. 
14 https://www.caiso.com/meetings-events/topics/market-surveillance-committee.

LS Power Comments 
Page 7 
 
to the overall health of the market.  It would add some discipline and oversight 
into stakeholder input and provide the Board with greater ability to understand 
and evaluate the merits of PJM and stakeholder proposals.  
IV. Enhancing State Participation in the Stakeholder Process 
LS Power has long supported expanded Section 205 rights for PJM states related to 
cost allocation for new transmission and supports ensuring the states have a 
meaningful way to participate in Board, PJM and stakeholder deliberations.  Given 
that there are 13 states and the District of Columbia, there is no single policy to 
incorporate into the PJM markets, unlike single-state RTOs.  It would undermine the 
independence of PJM and the Board to integrate a single state policy goal into the 
market rules of PJM.   
The states were intimately involved in the discussions involving the formation of 
PJM.  At that time, states did not want to be voting members because they did not 
want to be constrained by the rules governing stakeholders.  They wanted the ability 
to interface with PJM management and the Board outside of the stakeholder process.  
Some were also concerned that voting would give the appearance of prejudicing their 
primary role of ensuring wholesale prices are appropriately incorporated into state 
retail tariffs.  The concern was that it could prejudice the record if they were involved 
with the creation of these costs at the wholesale level.  They also did not want to 
participate directly in the RTO through a voting mechanism so that they could retain 
jurisdictional distinctions between the Commission and the states.15   
This reasoning still stands today.  Indeed, providing the States with a formal role in 
running PJM would add to the policy uncertainty that exists today.  As noted early 
in these comments, making multi-billion-dollar investments with several decades of 
useful life will require market structure durability and contract sanctity.  Both of 
those drivers of investment can be undermined by political pressure, which runs in 
four-year cycles and is not primarily focused on long-term market viability.   
To that point, PJM’s job is to run a market which in its basic terms matches supply 
to demand and produces a just and reasonable cost for the service.  The allocation of 
that cost then becomes a rate-making issue for the states, who rightly manage 
affordability constructs.  To a great extent, the states already can control those costs: 
for example, states control the physical siting for hyperscalers from building data 
centers in their states limiting demand, they can develop tariffs that ensure the 
hyperscalers pay their fair share for interconnection costs and retail service, and they 
 
15 https://www.eba-net.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/11-185-205.pdf

LS Power Comments 
Page 8 
 
can implement tariffs that protect other customers from costs created by the need to 
provide hyperscalers electricity.  But all of these roles would benefit from increased 
coordination.  Thus, LS Power strongly supports the process proposed by Chairman 
Bagot of Virginia and representatives of the data centers to develop model retail 
tariffs.16 
LS Power has examined other RTOs in the country for insight into the role of states.  
It is worth quoting an Energy Bar Association article that noted:  
“As regulators began practical consideration of an advisory role in regional 
wholesale markets, it is helpful to restate, in this context, how those markets 
fit with state regulation.  These answers take slightly different shapes in states 
with retail competition regimes and those with traditional vertically integrated 
regulatory systems”.  For example, in SPP, states have voting rights over some 
of SPP’s tariff while in MISO, the states have a purely advisory role and do 
not vote, even on transmission related issues.17   
Indeed, FERC itself has expressed concerns about the role of states in RTO 
governance as reported in a document prepared for NARUC:   
“Overall, the Final Rule allows for flexibility as to the appropriate role of the 
states in RTO governance and operation (after RTO development and 
formation), particularly in those few areas where the FERC does not intend to 
exercise exclusive authority under the Federal Power Act.  Stated another 
way, after RTO development and formation ... the role of the states in RTO 
governance and operation might tend to be mainly advisory in nature.”18 
Some potential changes: 
• The Commission could try to create a Federal-state Joint Board but that seems 
like a cumbersome approach at a time when fast action is demanded.   
 
16 https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/about-pjm/who-we-are/public-disclosures/2026/20260630-va-scc-and-
data-center-coalition-letter-re-cifp-connect-manage-reliability-backstop-procurement.pdf 
17 “The OMS Committee has the opportunity to provide input into the transmission planning, resource adequacy, 
and transmission cost allocation approach and processes, and may report periodically to MISO’s Board.” Agreement 
Of Transmission Facilities Owners To Organize The Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc., A Delaware 
Non-Stock Corporation, available at https://cdn.misoenergy.org/MISO%20TOA%20(for%20posting)47071.pdf   
Appendix F Section 6.3. 
18 Regional Transmission Organizations And The Coordination Of Regional Electricity Markets: A Review Of FERC 
Order 2000, Costello and Burns (2000) https://pubs.naruc.org/pub/FA860A98-9F87-51CE-66CB-99061504D141 , 
p.45

LS Power Comments 
Page 9 
 
Some recommendations: 
• Expand OPSI to include representatives of the governors.  PJM finds itself in 
a relatively new circumstance: some governors are concerned that their state 
utility commissions cannot fully represent their states’ interests. In response, 
an additional option would be to supplement OPSI by changing the OPSI 
composition to include two members from each state: a representative from 
the state’s utility commission and a representative nominated by the governor, 
which could be another commissioner but would not need to be.    This would 
address governors’ concerns that they are not being fully represented by 
allowing governors to appoint their own representative to participate on the 
committee.   LS Power supports enhancing OPSI to bring the politics and 
policy needs into discussions at the stakeholder level, rather than those needs 
being proffered in a manner that appears to be political pressure when the 
stakeholder process is complete.  OPSI would continue under its structure in 
terms of voting rules, etc.   
• The stakeholder process would benefit by enhancing the capability of all state 
representatives to more meaningfully participate in the stakeholder process.  
Members would provide additional funding to ensure OPSI’s staff include 
experts on electricity design who can participate in technical discussions.19  
Staffing an enhanced OPSI enables stakeholders to engage in substantive 
dialogue — at a minimum reaching mutual understanding of each other’s 
positions, and at best arrive at solutions that meet our shared objectives. OPSI 
would continue to have its rights to meet with the PJM Board, attend 
stakeholder meetings and bring proposals forward when supported by some 
threshold level of the committee (to be determined). This gives OPSI the 
opportunity to be even better positioned to provide the states’ views and 
meaningfully contribute to influencing how Members consider issues and the 
issues that are considered. 
• Enable OPSI to vote on cost allocation for new transmission (whether rebuild 
or regional).  There is precedent from SPP to consider, and LS Power would 
support a stronger OPSI, with Section 205 powers for transmission cost 
 
19 LS Power considered the option of a NESCOE type organization as is used in New England, but determined there 
is no need to create yet another organization that would require separate funding, delineation of responsibilities and 
obligations between such a new organization and OPSI.  Rather, the simplest and most efficient approach is to 
enable governors to achieve direct participation in the stakeholder process is to enhance OPSI.

LS Power Comments 
Page 10 
 
allocation proposals similar to the SPP Regional State Committee.20  Any such 
authority should be subject to some threshold level of consent.   
• Expand the Nominating Committee to include the president of OPSI to 
participate as a non-voting member in the deliberations.    
V. Making the Stakeholder Process More Efficient  
LS Power observes that the stakeholder process needs more discipline generally. LS 
Power thinks the specifics of that discipline are best left to stakeholders themselves, 
and FERC should not be distracted by delving into the details of such a process.  The 
Commission has in fact done exactly what is necessary:  issued a Show Cause Order 
under FPA section 206 “in order to ensure that PJM’s ongoing processes generate 
reforms that are sufficiently timely and comprehensive to address the concerns we 
identify today.”21 More direct involvement could distract the Commission from its 
primary role as an economic regulator and create unnecessary ex parte concerns, 
actually limiting the ability to informally discuss proposed changes with the 
Commission.  The Members have imposed such discipline before — the creation of 
the CIFP process is a good example22 — and can do it again. In fact, the focus of the 
PJM Liaison Committee meeting on July 13, 2026, was PJM governance.23 
There are guidelines to impose more discipline worth considering: 
• Limiting the number of educational sessions. Educational sessions should 
continue to be taped so that no one can claim they were unable to attend. (PJM 
does not currently record meetings, and we support continuing that approach 
for non-educational meetings).  
• At the MRC and Members Committee, attendees should arrive empowered to 
make final decision votes, including the ability to vote even if a proposal is 
amended on the floor — every time a representative must “go back” to their 
organization, that adds a month of delay to the process.  
 
20 https://www.ferc.gov/introductory-guide-participation-southwest-power-pool-processes:  LS Power notes that 
SPP is comprised of vertically integrated utilities so comparisons are limited. 
21 Order Instituting Proceeding Under Section 206 of the Federal Power Act, 195 FERC ¶61,211 (issued June 18, 
2026) ¶31.   The OA language cited in footnote 1 (Section 1.5.3 of the PJM Operating Agreement) could be used as 
the basis for the Show Cause order. 
22 PJM Manual 34: PJM Stakeholder Process, Section 8.6.4. 
23 https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/committees/lc/2026/20260713/20260713-agenda.pdf .

LS Power Comments 
Page 11 
 
• Proposals should be broken down into their individual components on which 
Members can vote; PJM should then address the “workability” of the 
components or any proposal based on them. 
We also suggest stakeholders consider the following questions that are offered for 
further discussion rather than as settled recommendations:  
• Consideration of a more explicit acknowledgement of a “jump ball” structure 
that exists in ISO-NE24 and which is implicitly available in the Operating 
Agreement.  The backbones for such an approach already exist, while not 
changing the current clear authority of the Members Committee:   “Nothing 
herein shall be construed as affecting in any way the right of the Members, 
acting pursuant to a vote of the Members Committee as specified in Operating 
Agreement, section 8.4, unilaterally to make an application to FERC for a 
change in any rate, charge, classification, tariff or service, or any rule or 
regulation related thereto, under section 205 of the Federal Power Act and 
pursuant to the rules and regulations promulgated by FERC thereunder, 
subject to the right of any Member that voted against such change in any rate, 
charge, classification, tariff or service, or any rule or regulation related 
thereto, in intervene in opposition to any such application.”25 
In making this right more explicit, the Members Committee of PJM would 
have its own legal counsel, just like NEPOOL within the New England 
stakeholder process. This would help ensure that the PJM Members and PJM 
Transmission Owners, with separate 205 filing rights over some issues, are 
operating within their own appropriate roles and better help resolve 
stakeholder conflicts.   It would also ensure an independent legal review for 
the Operating Agreement language filed at FERC, proper Members 
Committee consultation of PJM Transmission Owner 205 Filings as required 
under the PJM Operating Agreement today, and monitoring timing of 
stakeholder process. The counsel could provide an important check on any 
unruly Members. 
• Should voting at lower-level committees shift from affiliate-level voting to a 
single representative vote as is done at the senior committees? At minimum, 
we recommend that two votes be taken at lower committee meetings.  These 
votes are intended to help advance proposals to higher level committees, but 
 
24 NEPOOL Participants Agreement, Section 11.1.5.  
25 PJM Operating Agreement, Section 11.5(b)

LS Power Comments 
Page 12 
 
they also provide information with respect to likely support at higher level 
committees.  They can also inform the Board. 
V.  What the Commission Can Do 
LS Power commends the Commission for its proactive efforts and orders to ensure 
that each region of the country can meet the changing electricity demands.  That 
said, LS Power believes that it is not just a cumbersome governance problem that 
has caused PJM to struggle to meet these demands, but a confluence of a number of 
challenges, including the need to revise retail tariffs, to better manage 
interconnection and transmission upgrades, to expedite supply chains, and the need 
to have forcing mechanisms that enable bilateral contracts between hyperscalers and 
new generation in order to obtain financing.  None of these challenges are unique to 
a competitive market such as PJM.  Vertically integrated utilities cannot bypass the 
physical realities of the current grid and supply chains, and moreover, their business 
model shifts the risk of cost and over-procurement back to ratepayers.  This reality 
should not, however, impede the ability to make enhancements to PJM’s governing 
process, as we have suggested here. 
The Commission also has a critical role to play: it must act under its statutory 
authority as an economic regulator.  It, too, is an independent organization staffed 
by industry experts.26 This expertise enables the Commission to be the ultimate 
backstop in allowing the Board and PJM to make politically unpopular decisions in 
order to carry out their mission of ensuring reliability through competitive markets.   
 
 
 
26 “Further, it has been suggested that FERC has perhaps been too deferential to proposals coming from the RTOs 
and may not give sufficient weight to minority stakeholder concerns or market monitor comments when it assesses 
contested filings. Interviewees suggested that instead, FERC should approach RTO proposals with sufficient 
scrutiny and not overly rely on RTO independence, particularly because RTOs themselves may be in pursuit of 
multiple goals, including state policy targets that conflict with market efficiency.”  How the RTO Stakeholder 
Process Affects Market Efficiency, James, Jones, Kricke & Greane, R Street Policy Study No. 112 (October 2017), 
p. 18.

LS Power Comments 
Page 13 
 
In our comments, LS Power has endeavored to identify areas in the PJM’s 
governance structure that could be improved and provide specific recommendations 
that can be implemented without disrupting the need to focus all our attention on 
how we get new resources online as quickly as possible.  We look forward to 
working with the Commission and all interested parties to take advantage of the 
tremendous opportunities afforded us all to meet the energy demands of today and 
tomorrow.   
Respectfully submitted,  
 
/s/ Marjorie R. Philips  
Marjorie Rosenbluth Philips  
Senior Vice President, Wholesale Market
